He also had to consider Sybil’s parents. They were rather old-fashioned and might oppose the marriage if any scandal arose. Still, he felt sure that if he explained the whole situation, they would be the first to appreciate his motives. Everything therefore favored poison. It was safe, reliable, and quiet, and avoided unpleasant scenes, which, like most Englishmen, he strongly disliked.

“He knew absolutely nothing about poisons, however. The waiter seemed unable to find any books in the library except Ruff’s Guide and Bailey’s Magazine, so he searched the shelves himself. Eventually he found a beautifully bound Pharmacopoeia and Erskine’s Toxicology, edited by Sir Mathew Reid. Sir Mathew was President of the Royal College of Physicians and one of the Buckingham’s oldest members, having been elected by mistake for someone else. The error had so annoyed the Committee that when the intended candidate appeared, they unanimously rejected him. The technical language in both books confused Lord Arthur. He was beginning to regret neglecting his classical studies at Oxford when he discovered, in Erskine’s second volume, a detailed and interesting description of aconitine written in reasonably clear English. It appeared to be exactly what he needed. According to the account, it worked quickly, almost instantly, caused no pain, and tasted quite acceptable when enclosed in a gelatin capsule, as Sir Mathew recommended. He noted the stated fatal quantity on his shirt cuff, returned the books to the shelves, and walked up St. James’s Street to Pestle and Humbey’s, the distinguished pharmacy. Mr. Pestle, who always served aristocratic customers himself, was surprised by the request and respectfully murmured that a doctor’s certificate was required. Lord Arthur explained that he needed it for a large Norwegian mastiff showing early signs of rabies. The dog had already bitten the coachman twice on the calf and had to be destroyed. This explanation completely satisfied Mr. Pestle. He praised Lord Arthur’s remarkable knowledge of poisons and had the prescription prepared immediately.

“Lord Arthur placed the capsule in a pretty little silver sweets box he spotted in a Bond Street shop window. He threw away Pestle and Hambey’s unattractive pillbox and drove straight to Lady Clementina’s.

Mrs. Clay’s feelings had overcome her self-interest. For the young man’s sake, she had given up the chance to keep pursuing Sir Walter. But she has talents as well as feelings, and it remains uncertain whose cunning will ultimately prevail. Having prevented her from becoming Sir Walter’s wife, he may eventually find himself flattered and caressed into making her Lady William instead.

Sir Walter and Elizabeth were undoubtedly shocked and humiliated by their companion’s departure and by discovering how mistaken they had been about her. They could turn to their important cousins for comfort, of course. Still, they would long feel that flattering and attending others, without receiving flattery and attention themselves, supplied only half the pleasure.

Anne quickly became satisfied that Lady Russell intended to love Captain Wentworth as he deserved. After that, only one thing diminished her happiness: she had no relatives to offer him whom a sensible man could esteem. She felt her inferiority in this respect keenly. Their unequal fortunes meant nothing to her and caused not a moment’s regret. But she had no family capable of welcoming and appreciating him properly, no respectability, harmony, or goodwill to return for the worth and immediate warmth she found among his brothers and sisters. This caused as much pain as she could feel amid circumstances otherwise so happy. She had only two friends to add to his circle, Lady Russell and Mrs. Smith. He, however, was entirely willing to become attached to both. Despite all Lady Russell’s past offenses, he could now sincerely value her. Provided he was not required to say that she had been right to separate them originally, he was ready to say almost anything else in her favor. Mrs. Smith, meanwhile, had several claims upon his friendship, enough to secure it quickly and permanently.

“Her recent kindness to Anne would have been sufficient on its own. Their marriage gave her two friends instead of depriving her of one. She was their first visitor after they settled into married life. Captain Wentworth helped her recover her husband’s property in the West Indies, writing letters, acting on her behalf, and guiding her through every small obstacle. With the energy of a fearless man and a determined friend, he fully repaid the help she had given his wife, or had ever intended to give her.

The studio was steeped in the rich fragrance of roses. Whenever the soft summer breeze moved through the garden trees, the open doorway admitted the heavy perfume of lilacs or the subtler sweetness of the pink-blossomed thorn.

Reclining in a corner of the divan made of Persian saddle-bags, and smoking his customary endless succession of cigarettes, Lord Henry Wotton could just glimpse the shining laburnum blossoms, honey-coloured and honey-sweet. Its quivering boughs seemed scarcely strong enough to support so flame-like a beauty. From time to time the fanciful shadows of flying birds crossed the long tussore-silk curtains drawn before the great window, creating a fleeting Japanese impression. They recalled to him those pale, jade-faced artists of Tokyo who strive, through a necessarily motionless art, to suggest speed and movement. The bees’ sulky humming, as they pushed through the tall uncut grass or circled persistently about the dusty golden horns of the wandering woodbine, only deepened the oppressive quiet. London’s muted roar resembled the low sustained note of a far-off organ.

At the room’s centre, fastened to an upright easel, stood a full-length painting of a young man of exceptional beauty. A short distance in front sat its painter, Basil Hallward, whose abrupt disappearance some years before had aroused such public excitement and prompted so many curious speculations.

Contemplating the graceful, handsome figure he had reflected so skilfully in his work, the artist smiled with pleasure, and the smile seemed ready to remain. Suddenly, however, he sprang up, shut his eyes, and pressed his fingers against their lids, as if trying to hold within his mind some strange dream from which he dreaded waking.

“This is your finest work, Basil, the finest thing you have ever painted,” Lord Henry said lazily. “You must send it to the Grosvenor next year. The Academy is far too big and vulgar. Whenever I visit, either there are so many people that I cannot see the pictures, which is dreadful, or so many pictures that I cannot see the people, which is worse. The Grosvenor really is the only choice.”

“I doubt I shall send it anywhere,” he replied, flinging back his head with that peculiar movement that had made his Oxford friends laugh.
